The Advocate seeks pitches and submissions for our forthcoming spring issues! Please see below for details.

The Advocate Special Ground & Groundless Issue
(Pitches Due by March 15th)

In the Poetics of Relation, Édouard Glissant claims we must “renew the visions and aesthetics of relating to the earth.” The forthcoming issue of the Advocate seeks to exhibit experiments in such visions and aesthetics by focusing on the theme of ground and groundlessness.

For our spring issue, the Advocate is seeking writing of all genres that engage with ground, grounds, and grounding. Spanning the material and the metaphysical, the ground or soil beneath our feet, where we bury our dead and the food required for life, points to the root of things, it is that upon which all else is built. The foundation. The rationale. The unbroken.

We invite engagements with this theme in various forms, including but not limited to poetry, fiction, experimental nonfiction, reviews, interviews, personal essays, and adapted scholarly research. We invite broad interpretations of Ground and Groundlessness, including ecocriticism, issues of sovereignty and statehood, memory studies, immigration and diaspora, and beyond.

The Advocate also welcomes unthemed submissions on a rolling basis!

Please email your pitches to advocate@cunydsc.org.

By Yagiz Ay

Lulu. Do we have to go out tonight? My nerves are bad and I am uncertain. I see a hundred flowers but not one that I can touch. I drift into dullness and mourn the horror of growing old. The morning of life was the best in its juvenile purity. The dampness of furs, the scent of rain-soaked leaves. The eerie fragrance of childhood scenes. The sun flooded us with intervals. Seduced by flowers, corals and the shimmer of shells. I talked to cousin Margaret among the colored-fish. The water was cold like a jewel. Papa said, Augusta, come, warm beside the fire. At night I listened the fireplace crack to the beat of a perishing moon. The birds charmed me at daybreak. I guess, we are going to that party after all. Odious and engulfed with absurdity, these nouveau riche. No taste left in gowns or lingerie. But the one marrying, to that dismal Schön, was you. Your white dress and razor black hair condemned the night, inadequate. I stammered and bit my lip. How did I keep my act serene? We tangoed to the incantation of an inner pull. A wave swept over my head. My hair set free, our eyes met. You can’t put a butterfly in a jar. Then there was the trial. On the run for mariticide. I asked about you meanwhile. No one spared, the stubborn opined: you were the ruin of all love. In your permeating fugitive gleam, you are the only one who can save me, you said. I did not have the courage to reply: “let’s forever leave this town.” I handed the passport and said: you play the Countess for a while. After sickness, care, and defeat. I mourn the last thing to come out of the box. As your sight and the century collapse into an echo.

 

Murder. SIR – We have all witnessed in recent years the resurgence of that stupendous claim on the pages of this very magazine, first voiced in an article by Mr. R. P. Daggers titled “MURDER – is it art?” Mr. Daggers insists, nay, provokes the readers of this fine magazine to contemplate a tempting and ludicrous proposal scorched in the lowliest confines of the human mind. By Jove, inferno has no terror for him. It is my wish here, sir, to intrude, and to reverse the salience of this claim now well-known and well-discussed in every coffeehouse in London. For it only takes a child’s knowledge to prove Mr. Daggers’ lewdsuggestions wrong and to demonstrate with Logic how the opposite is closer to the truth. I am positive that murder is not an art, as these murder-fanciers like Mr. Daggers have it, but art is a kind of murder. When an artist of esteemed character engages in an act dissecting the vicissitudes and the harshness of the times he finds he is handed a demonic power. A power, sir, from the most deep pits of hell that knows no limits other than its own which appears to every artist as instinct and a mystery. The great Shakespeare knew it well – as did his coterie of famed murderers, Macbeth and Caesar, Hamlet and Anthony, Othello and Richard. So did Milton, Pope, Swift, Gray, Warsh, King, Hammond, Gay, Rowe, Young, Mallet, Broome, Garth, Morel, Parnell and Akenside. With this sultry power the artist grants himself a charter to favor the embellishments of art over the pangs of life. The finest portrait painter of our age, Mr. Gainsborough, takes a soul each time he puts his hands on that sublime canvas of his. Who remembers these men and women that feature in his fair paintings? They are to us no more than mere decorations whose origin is long gone and unlikely to come back. They are little but the men and women of Mr. Gainsborough. He imprisoned their spirit in the crux of his artifice. Now, you might say, what of others? Is Mr. Constable a murderer because he painted an empty landscape, Nature’s finest gift? Mais bien sur! Mr. Constable is no frivolous artist, sir, and his beautiful strokes are enough reason to see that this man has the bloody instinct to kill life itself. To create a painting so great, our own pitiful lives are destroyed by its sheer beauty. His gift, what the French name genie, is his fatal blade. He loves Nature sacrilegiously, thus, he kills it. I shall conclude with a brief indulgence, which I could not forebear to disclose. As we are vastly familiar, Mr Wordsworth, whose worthy acquaintance I had the pleasure of making, wrote a fine poem which included the line “we murder to dissect.” We are free to express doubt whether we dispute Mr Wordsworth’s suggestion that Art and Science are but barren leaves, yet the Lake poet’s words are wise as pearls. This, sir, is the age of murder. Its muse is Envy and its weapon is Avarice. State and gravity are trivial affairs in face of its design, and the pre-destination it charted is in a lock. Art is men’s tool of revenge against the life which has rendered him very helpless and very wretched. The false wit of Mr. Daggers thereof is mere noise for us to resist as seamen and sea-farers – who for undisclosed reasons are well-acquainted with the concept of murder – ought resist the temptation to drink.

 

Nude Descending a Staircase, No. 2. No I do not ever descend. Ever descend he ask and I do not I ever descend. I ask ever I do descend and he ask if no ever descend. Do ask not I and I ask no ever descend. Ever I ask how precise he precise ask he do not ever precise ask. Descend not precise, precise not descend. If ever I descend I ask precise not I ask if I do not ever descend and I ask precise. If descend precise and ever precise I ask ever descend I. Descend ever stair I. Not I. Stair he. Stair he me. Stair he. Stair it. Stair do not. Stair descend. Stair ask. Ask stair. I do stair. Ask stair. Stair descend. Descend do. Stair a case. Ever case. Nu-Case. Du-case. Do case. Ever case. Precise case. Case-case. Case I do. Stair I nu. Mar-nu. Two.

No. 2
Do. 2
Nu two
Du to
No to
Des to.
Cen to
a stair.
Clair.

by Addy Malinowski

“zionism is the leading cause of death in Palestine”

— Mohammed El-Kurd

I am writing this from Bay Ridge, Brooklyn, the heart of New York City’s “little Palestine,” the Levant of Long Island, on the third night of the so-called Gaza ceasefire—or rather, the shift to a phase of “managed genocide” as Ramy Abdu recently put it in The Intercept. The zionist regime has already murdered at least seven Palestinians since the start of the ceasefire, five by drone strike, and one by gunfire—though surely the number is higher than reported. With only cruelty to match his capriciousness, Trump has declared that just half of UN aid trucks will be allowed to enter the Gaza Strip. It remains an astonishing fact of human history that the fate of so many can be dictated by the whims of a psychopathic few.

Any “peace” worth the name should begin with the zionist governing coalition put in prison and placed on trial by an international tribunal for crimes against humanity. A serious reckoning would furthermore require a full investigation into the complicity of the Biden and Trump administrations, attended by an audit of every major Western media outlet for crimes of deception and genocidewashing, as well as a full accounting of the death and destruction in Gaza, which will most certainly reveal casualties in the hundreds of thousands. Last, a thorough peace necessitates the immediate demilitarization of the zionist regime, including a decommission of their unaccounted for nuclear program, the largest in the region.

That these are not the prerequisites for “peace”—let alone decolonization and the actualization of Palestinian self-determination—guarantees that the zionist and American regimes are interested only in taking a pause from regularly scheduled mass-slaughter in order to shore up zionism’s reputation across the world, which is at historic lows, even amongst historically amnesiac Americans. In the words of John Mearsheimer, “Their reputation has been sullied forever.” The larger strategic aim for the Americans is to initiate a renewed effort at economic and diplomatic normalization between the zionist regime and Arab states, the Gulf states in particular. “It is through this process of normalization,” write the authors of Resisting Erasure, “that the US seeks to reassert primacy in the region.” In other words, it’s time for the US vassal to dial down its genocide in order to resume economic integration with the Gulf states and shore up waning American hegemony in the region. The success of the Trump-brokered Abraham Accords is also on the table, with the Saudi holdout—contingent on the recognition of Palestinian statehood—remaining the last roadblock to normalization.

Fundamentally, zionism is at the heart of US policy in the region; Al-Aqsa Flood drove a stake into this heart on October 7. The world now knows, after two years of genocide, that the depths of the sickness stem not only from Jerusalem, but from Washington, London, Berlin, and Brussels, too. Across the world, the sentiment is the same; that Everybody Hates Israel¹ has been elevated to collective affect, a powerfully potent political feeling, felt across the South as well as by critics in the North. For this I am grateful.

For us at The Graduate Center, this odium righteously abides. Zionists have been relegated to a tiny minority in the Doctoral and Graduate Students’ Council and Palestine solidarity events are held without incident across many programs and departments. CUNY Central, however, along with the GC’s comprador administrators, remain repressive and vindictive, as evidenced by chancellor Matos’ testimony to the US congress in July and the continuing attempts to silence the “Fired Four” at Brooklyn College—not to mention continued consequences for undergraduates who participated in the CUNY Gaza Solidarity Encampment in the spring of 2024. Nationally, the federal government, with the aid of zionist megadonors and Israeli puppet organizations², is enforcing a “new McCarthyism” across college campuses and civil society, punishing those who dare to speak in defense of Palestinian liberation, eroding long-held US first-amendment protections, and so-called academic freedom at large, with perps labeled first as anti-Semites, then as terrorists, and now, as “antifa.”

It is in precisely this political context, when risks are on the rise, that graduate students must refuse to silence themselves. Now is also not the time to fall back on an easy “politics of appeal,” designed to appease institutions and liberal skeptics. Sadly, academics are prone to rely on an appeal to “higher authorities,” whether that be a supervisor, a hiring committee, or those with “prestigious” academic affiliation; this is especially true in an academic economy that manufactures scarcity which in turn produces obsequiousness to the conciliatory tendencies of those who hold sway in the profession.

For Mohammed El-Kurd, author of Perfect Victims and the Politics of Appeal, elements of a “politics of appeal” in the context of Palestine solidarity includes deference to citing international law and legal frameworks; privileging the invented category of the “civilian” casualty, which necessarily eclipses the grievability of those who “resist” (which on some level includes all Palestinians, including the armed resistance); attempts to “humanize” the Palestinian; appeals to dual American or European citizenship; and perhaps most importantly for El-Kurd’s argument, appeals to the Palestinian’s ability to condemn anti-Semitism and separate Judaism from zionism.

These appeals, for El-Kurd, constitute “perfect victimhood.” To be slaughtered, live on all our phones and televisions, is not enough evidence. Palestinians, El-Kurd argues, must prove, in order to receive sympathy from a Western audience, their a priori innocence of a crime for which they can hardly be impugned: anti-Semitism. In Perfect Victims and often in his media appearances, El-Kurd tells the story of how his childhood home in Sheikh Jarrah was violently occupied by Jewish settlers from Brooklyn in 2009. “Here is where I stand,” he writes. “There is a Jew who lives, by force, in half of my home in Jerusalem, and he does so by ‘divine decree,’ in the name of the Jewish people.” The reality, and this should come as no great surprise to anyone, is that in occupied Palestine, Jewish life is treated as exponentially greater than that of the Palestinian. “It is not my fault they are Jewish,” writes El-Kurd.

No, it is not the Palestinian’s fault that zionist tanks that demolish Palestinian homes and centuries-old olive trees have the Star of David on the side. It is not the Palestinian’s fault that zionist warplanes with the Star of David drop bombs with “death to Arabs” written in Sharpie on the side. It is not the Palestinian’s fault that, in 2023, Jewish police officers branded, with hot iron, the Star of David on the cheek of Orwa Sheikh Ali in Jerusalem. Rather, Palestinians have gone above and beyond to make clear the distinction between Judaism and zionism, all while the self-proclaimed Jewish state is happy to weaponize this conflation, using the charge of anti-Semitism as a cudgel against its critics.

Even if all Palestinians were raging Jew haters, it still wouldn’t justify slaughtering them all. Here at CUNY, those of us in the Palestine solidarity movement are all anti-Semites, as far as the university and the state are concerned. The brilliance of El-Kurd’s provocation to activists is this: why continue to play into what amounts to a red herring, a rhetorical trapping designed to incriminate? If we are all anti-Semites, terrorists, antifa—well, so what?

In The Battle of Algiers, the French commander Mathieu skillfully uses the Parisian press corps as mouthpiece of colonial governance in Algiers, manipulating the flow of information to the metropole and discrediting the armed resistance, laying blame for Algier’s suffering on the FLN—much in the same way the zionist regime’s media proxies in the West shamelessly discredit the armed resistance in Gaza as well as zionism’s critics abroad. It is a key strategic objective of an occupying force to tightly control the organs of communication and the flows of information; perception and attitudes are key. It does us well to refuse to play by the same terms of debate. Our students, working class New Yorkers and from immigrant families, most of all, understand when their instructors speak the truth about injustice, and respect when we do so. The genocide is a fact. That this is a zionist, as well as American genocide, is a fact. All else is distraction.

In the penultimate chapter of Perfect Victims, El-Kurd asks, are we indeed all Palestinians? referencing the popular protest chant that can be heard throughout the streets of New York since fall 2023. Are we indeed all Palestinians, in our thousands, our millions? El-Kurd juxtaposes his experience at street protests in New York and London with the living horror throughout occupied Palestine that Palestinians are subjected to, in the Gaza killbox, in zionist prisons, and in front of a policeman’s gun. Yet, El-Kurd writes, it is too tempting, “almost comforting,” to indulge in one’s guilt. “Gaza has the right to forsake us, to never forgive us, to spit in our faces,” he writes. “How many of us stutter when asked about resistance, or disavow our right to resist entirely, our need to resist? How many of us choose our careers over our kin? How many of us could have done something, anything, and did not?”

When El-Kurd proposes that the rallying cry we are all Palestinians must “abandon the metaphor and manifest materially,” how do we respond? What does it mean to “embody the Palestinian condition?” Certainly, after two years of genocide, the moment demands that we interrogate the “pretenses that absolve us from participating in history” and “renew our commitment to the truth, to spitting the truth, unflinchingly, unabashedly”—but we must also go beyond the truth. How will we do so?

 

Notes

  1. see “Everybody Hates the Police” by Jonathan Flatley on how after the murder of George Floyd hatred toward the police became a powerful organizing force, bringing collectivities of police-haters across the globe together in a struggle against racism, capital, and state repression. Flatley refers to police-hatred as a “vital affect.” For more on how powerful Israel-hatred is, and how affecting images of the slaughter from inside Gaza have been on the global populace, one can look to the concern around, for instance, pro-Palestinian narratives on TikTok, the world’s most popular social media platform, and the praise which zionist billionaire Larry Ellison received upon purchasing the platform in September. 
  2. Al-Jazeera’s exposé on how the zionist lobby functions on US and UK college campuses is insightful, though its influence on student groups is only the lower limit of the overall reach of the lobby on administrators, donors, politicians, and so forth.

by Job Miller

The University does not support the change we desire. It is all too willing to maintain its fiscal investments in the economy of exploitation and destruction that the current world-system thrives upon. The administrators buckle and bend to open up campuses to the hyper-policing and forms of control so essential to neoliberalism. This is not new; the collusion of the University with the war machine can be traced at every point of the last century, from the gladhanding of the Department of Defense to the campus-infiltration of the CIA.

I am suspicious that the practices we take up as scholars, teachers, and critics in the University cannot help but bolster the very system which has oppressed us. In many moments this happens against our will, of course; but what I want to emphasize is how our investment in the University makes us complicit in its machinery of subtler repressions. Too often we allow the University to transform our thinking and desire by determining our relation to the text, to art and its inherent capacity to generate resistance. By overvaluing the University, even when it is assailed by reaction, we ignore the sinister constraints that it imposes on all of us.

I spent several years pursuing a PhD at Columbia. I spent much of that time turning in assignments far too late and of rather poor quality. It was here that my suspicion solidified that the University had no capacity to facilitate upheaval, none of the incendiary potential necessary for the dominant order to be unmade. As a teacher, I felt that the majority of my work merely taught students a set of analytical tools that could be used to blunt what was truly radical or destabilizing. Teaching George Jackson is fine and dandy, but I don’t really give a fuck if some private equity kid feels a little guilt as they plow forward in their career of exploitation and global dispossession. Worse was that I became convinced that teaching these texts became a vaccine against students’ capacity to be disrupted. Against all my intentions, such classes served to insulate these students from the world around them. We must face the University’s awesome power to invert our best intentions, to steer the content of even the most radical class into a pro forma fulfillment of the credentialed and the chosen. To ignore this process is a weakness that has rendered much of our critical work fangless, inherently flawed.

As a student at Columbia my frustration thickened. The place was afflicted by a rampant competitiveness that resulted in a space hostile to those fragile ideas which require delicate nuance to be enunciated. When we orient ourselves to the text with the crushing pressure of publication we develop a relationship to the text that is neither generative nor made in good faith. The command to write, when we have not spent enough time being humble before a text, shuts down the potential for it to overwhelm us. Then mindlessly we parrot this same demand to students who are not given enough time to consider what it is they begin to chew up and regurgitate. It is no wonder that AI becomes a viable response to this demand to produce at all costs. There is a warped relation to the text that speaks only of the fulfillment of an economic epistemology of value and exploitation. Is overwhelming ecstasy and terror not our original relation to art? Is this not the basis for our desire? Is this not what reminds us, despite the pain it brings, that the world is not as full as it could be? Instead we are driven by the pressures of the academy to perform the song and dance of “mastery.” This need to make everything not merely useful but marketable carries within it the rancid stench of double exploitation—wherein the text and ourselves are mangled. Thus when we are grinding away for the University we become merely the forerunners of the machine which seeks to make all things searchable; we become spinners of terms, crafters of keywords. It is such an unpleasantly disdainful task, a supremely silly game to play. Even those that don’t get caught up immediately are quickly digested by those who come after into fodder for the competitive-class to engorge upon. It may sound despondent to understand our work as hurrying the commodification of what is radical, but should we not face the truth of it? We are living in a time of defeat. The strategies of consumption and commodification reach deeper at every moment into the bodies of resistance. We have not intellectualized our way out. It is dark, and we are much in need of hope.

When I started out at community college I did not know what I wanted to study. I did not know terms or theory. But I did have humility and a burning desire to speak. I sensed a secret way of knowing that made me ache when I read something which was greater than myself, a sensation that made me bend before it. I possessed a certain orientation as the result of growing up poor, and of experiencing the pain of loss and the frustration of helplessness in adolescence. But I also knew the love that comes as the last resort—when there is nothing left to give piecemeal and when to give anything at all is to give everything. The glimpses available in reading grew into the conviction of study. It was not enough to have felt mere moments of liberation. It became necessary to inhabit the text as a space of refuge—as a location from which to imagine the terror and freedom beyond horizons which I had not yet known existed. Study was an act that breathed life into me as it offered a vision of the future which was no longer rooted in what job or career or path to wealth might be in store, but announced success in the form of a new world wherein my labor was returned to me, and in the joy of chasing the questions of what it means to live expanded. It was a difficult task to hold onto this conviction even as it was the only reason I could manage to write anything insightful. Even on this lower plane of academic prestige the models of study were afflicted by those too scared to admit that the task of study is irruptive. I desired recognition. I desired the aristocratic flair and grace of the language which spread itself across so much of what is written. It was difficult to know what the academy would want me to forfeit. So much of my engagement with the University was a sweet freedom from what seemed to limit me. Poverty seemed to be washed off from me as I displayed a certain mastery of the texts around me. These are the devastating trappings that became heavier the further I moved along the line of professionalism. Though the absurdity of studying literature at community college cannot be discounted, sharing in a working-class desire to do something that had no practical elaboration had its small joys. This study was not desperate to prove its value. It found its reward in the text; in sharing it. It demanded all and the reward was in shifting moments a glimpse of freedom and beauty. It was hope for something more.

Others find this absurdity of study from differing positions. This is what drives us to read. It connects us. It is what we share, but also what turns around and elaborates our difference, an individuating force, an expression of becoming that can only announce itself as the specific. This willingness and compulsion to risk it all fosters a relationship to the text that is on a radically different plane than that of the exploitative use-based commodity, desperate in its grasp for mastery. Of course this isn’t exclusive or a secret—it just requires true risk. And this risk means also risking one’s place in the academy, that machine of consumption and nullification. The University does not foster the space for this risky relation to the text, to study, to each other: we must look beyond it.

This is the reason for the titular question. Do we need to imagine its end? Do we need to imagine a different relation to each other? What does it look like to study trenchantly outside of its limitations and motivations? We need relief from this ugliness. We need to collect ourselves. We need to remember that we read because literature, art, reveals a desire beyond what the forces of order tell us we have. Do we read and study to publish? To gain postdoc positions? To secure tenure track jobs? To show how much we control the text? We have been trained to forget how far we reach, how unstable we are. It is a goddamn shame to read to produce criticism, etc., which has as its goal the opposite, namely, to make everything extra legible so that we learn and then teach how to avoid that messy sticky turmoil which is why we read in the first place. Many within the University are susceptible to its trappings. All that they engage with suffers from banality and stupidity. They can not articulate anything interesting. They cannot see past the walls meant to keep the rabble out. But what if we are the rabble let in accidentally? An undercommons is fine, but I would have much much more. We must remember this is not for us. We must remember that we desire something else entirely.

a poem by Andrea E. Beck

In the waiting room
we sit.
Rough upholstery
scratching our bare legs
The clock resoundingly ticking
as the minutes drag by.
Waiting to be seen.
Do you view us
as a whole
or as individuals?
Are we only a copay,
an appointment to be kept?
Red, and yellow, black and white
we are precious in HIS sight.
Our stories can aid
your understanding of us.
It is not just about the symptoms
our symptoms,
but also about the pain
our pain,
Physically
Emotionally
Spiritually.
It is about where we have been
which should not be negated.
So I will
take a number,
wait in line,
as I reflect on who I am
and pray that you see me,
the person
not just the problem.
